rationale: B wins because its lanes are cleaner. "Going puts its AI planner behind the paywall — with 2 million free members watching" is a real business-model story, and "Mistake fares vanish fast — Going's AI wants the trip planned before they do" gives a separate consumer protagonist. A has sharper teeth in places, but "$200 mistake fare" is invented and "turns ... into a booked week" walks straight into the no-booking fact; that is how a useful strategy doc becomes a correction.
gaps_in_A: "$200 mistake fare" invents a fare price. The update gives no dollar amount; fake specificity is worse than vagueness.
"turns a $200 mistake fare into a booked week" overpromises around booking. The supplied facts say no airline or hotel booking happens in-app.
"the free tier finds the fare, the paid tier tells you what to do with it" assumes free users receive the same fare alert. The facts only say Going has free members and the planner is Premium-only.
The first two kept angles overlap around the same paywall/freemium tension: "for paying members only" and "A fraction of them get the trip" are different desks, but not fully different stories.
gaps_in_B: "Mistake fares vanish fast" is plausible travel lore, but it is not in the supplied facts. If the urgency matters, source it or frame it as a question.
"category-creation" is puffed-up altitude for a feature extension. Prove a category is forming or call it an alerts-to-planning product shift.
"the entire value case for the paid tier" overstates the $550 claim. The update says paid members save an average on booked flights, not that this number carries the whole tier or the new planner.
"journalist-fit-check" as the next step is premature for the no-booking and data angles; those need live agentic-booking coverage, paid-base size, or $550 methodology first.
